items.title: WWI was triggered by a wrong turn
items.claim: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand survived the first assassination attempt that morning. What caused the second, successful attempt hours later?

options.text: A coordinated second wave of assassins ambushed his motorcade on the way to the hospital
His driver took a wrong turn into a side street, stalled the car, and stopped directly in front of Gavrilo Princip
Princip followed the motorcade by tram and intercepted it at the town hall
A Serbian double agent inside the security detail signalled his location

items.reveal_title: A wrong turn into world war
items.reveal:
After a bomb attack that morning failed, the Archduke insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital. His driver, Leopold Lojka, had not been told the route had been changed. He turned right onto Franz Joseph Street, was told he was going the wrong way, and stalled while reversing.

Gavrilo Princip, who had given up and was eating a sandwich (the sandwich story is disputed but he was at Schiller's delicatessen), happened to be standing there. He stepped forward and fired twice from five feet away.
items.why: The 'causes of WWI' essay tends to load every variable onto structural forces (alliances, militarism, imperialism). Those forces created the powder keg, but a stalled car lit the fuse. Contingency matters.

items.title: Pope Urban II launched the First Crusade in 1095
items.claim: What did Pope Urban II do at the Council of Clermont on 27 November 1095?

options.text: He banned all warfare among Christians
He called on Western Christians to take the cross and recover Jerusalem from the Seljuk Turks, offering remission of sin to those who fought — launching what became the First Crusade (1096-99)
He excommunicated all kings of Europe
He convened only to discuss church reform

items.reveal:
Urban's speech at Clermont survives in four contemporary versions, all written years later. The crowd reportedly responded 'Deus vult!' — God wills it. The motive came partly from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos's appeal for help after Seljuk advances after the Battle of Manzikert (1071).

The First Crusade (1096-99) captured Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (15 July 1099) after a massacre of inhabitants. Crusader states (Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli, the Kingdom of Jerusalem) were established.

Subsequent crusades (Second 1147-49, Third 1189-92, Fourth sacked Constantinople 1204) showed the institution's instability. Jerusalem fell to Saladin in 1187. The last Crusader holding, Acre, fell in 1291.
items.why: The Crusades were a centuries-long phenomenon launched by a single papal speech that promised salvation for warfare. The collision they began (Western Christianity, Byzantine Christianity, Islam, Judaism) reshaped the medieval Mediterranean.

items.title: Most Roman emperors died violently
items.claim: Of the 69 Roman emperors from Augustus (27 BCE) to Theodosius I (395 CE), how many died of natural causes?

options.text: Almost all — emperors were generally well-protected
Roughly a third — the rest died by assassination, in battle, by suicide or under suspicious circumstances
All emperors after Nero were murdered

items.reveal:
Joseph Saleh and colleagues (2019) modelled imperial deaths and found violent end rates above 50% for the first 25 years of any reign. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284) saw around 50 emperors and usurpers in 50 years.

Named assassinations: Caligula (41), Claudius (54, probably poisoned by Agrippina), Domitian (96), Commodus (192), Caracalla (217), Elagabalus (222) and many more. Some died in war (Decius at Abrittus, 251; Valerian captured by the Persians, 260).
items.why: The imperial succession looks orderly from the list of names. Statistically, becoming emperor was one of the most dangerous jobs in the ancient world — which itself shaped imperial policy.
